explanations.explanation: Conspiring is the charge, friend. Amaziah sends word to the king that “Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel.” (Amos 7:10) Notice that's Amaziah's description of Amos, in Amaziah's own message. He didn't send a note about a parking dispute. He went straight for the big word.

Nothing about stealing shows up in his message. Amaziah tells the king that “Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel.” (Amos 7:10) The charge is conspiring, and it's aimed at the king himself. Nobody is counting the temple silverware in this passage.

The Sabbath doesn't come up anywhere in these verses. The message Amaziah sends to Jeroboam says “Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel.” (Amos 7:10) That's a charge about the king, not about a day of rest. Nobody even checked a calendar, friend.

By the sword is right. Amaziah tells the king that Amos said, “Jeroboam will die by the sword…” (Amos 7:11) Notice whose report this is: it's what Amaziah passes along to Jeroboam. This one is a heavy line, so I'll just read it plainly and leave the jokes in the oven.

Old age isn't in the report. Amaziah tells the king that Amos said, “Jeroboam will die by the sword…” (Amos 7:11) The words are about a sword, not about a long life. This is a heavy line, so I'll keep it simple and say it straight.

Illness isn't mentioned in Amaziah's report. He says Amos declared, “Jeroboam will die by the sword…” (Amos 7:11) The same sentence goes on to talk about Israel going into exile. It's a heavy part of the story, so I'll read it plainly and move along.

Exile it is. The report says, “Israel will surely go into exile, away from their homeland.” (Amos 7:11) Exile means being sent away from your own country, and the words “away from their homeland” sit right there in the same line. That line explains itself, friend, which saves me a lot of work.

Battle isn't the word in the report. It says, “Israel will surely go into exile, away from their homeland.” (Amos 7:11) The sword does show up earlier in that same verse, for Jeroboam, so I see why battle sounds close. But this blank is about leaving home, not about a fight.

Hiding is a natural guess, but it's not what Amaziah reports. He says Amos declared, “Israel will surely go into exile, away from their homeland.” (Amos 7:11) Hiding means ducking down close to home. I can hide behind a flour sack and still be in my own bakery, but exile means leaving home altogether.

Judah is the place. Amaziah tells Amos, “Go away, you seer! Flee to the land of Judah; earn your bread there and do your prophesying there.” (Amos 7:12) He even names the destination. Amos didn't have to pick a spot, because the priest picked it for him.

Egypt is a famous place in the Bible, but it isn't the one named here. Amaziah says, “Flee to the land of Judah…” (Amos 7:12) He tells Amos to do his prophesying there. So Amos's travel plans came with the destination already filled in.

Moab is a real place, but Amaziah doesn't send Amos there. He says, “Flee to the land of Judah; earn your bread there and do your prophesying there.” (Amos 7:12) Judah is the one name in his sentence. Amaziah had his answer ready, and it wasn't Moab.

Amaziah gives the reason right in the same breath: “But never prophesy at Bethel again, because it is the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom.” (Amos 7:13) So the reason he states is that Bethel belongs to the king. He calls it the king's sanctuary and the temple of the kingdom. That's the reason in his own words, and he doesn't add anything else.

explanations.answer: It is a city of refuge
explanations.explanation: Amaziah never calls Bethel a city of refuge. He says it is “the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom.” (Amos 7:13) He's sending Amos out of the place, not inviting him in. A refuge is where you run for safety, and the priest is pointing Amos toward the exit.

Amaziah gives no such description. What he says is that Bethel is “the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom.” (Amos 7:13) It's the king's place, in his words. A school would be a nice idea, but nobody is handing out diplomas in this passage.

Amos says something quite different. He tells Amaziah, “I was not a prophet,” and adds, “nor was I the son of a prophet; rather, I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees.” (Amos 7:14) So “always a prophet” doesn't match what he says about himself. His old work was with flocks and fig trees.

False is right. Amos tells Amaziah, “I was not a prophet,” and then, “nor was I the son of a prophet; rather, I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees.” (Amos 7:14) That's not the résumé you'd expect for a prophet, if you ask me. Then again, my own résumé says stamper, so I'm in no position to judge.

The LORD is the one. Amos says, “But the LORD took me from following the flock and said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to My people Israel.’” (Amos 7:15) Amaziah just told him to go away, and Amos answers by saying who sent him. Not a king, not a priest, just the LORD. I'd call that a pretty complete answer.

King Uzziah isn't named anywhere in these verses. Amos says, “But the LORD took me from following the flock and said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to My people Israel.’” (Amos 7:15) The only king in this scene is Jeroboam, and he's the one Amaziah wrote to (Amos 7:10). The one giving Amos the assignment is the LORD.

King Hezekiah doesn't appear in this passage at all. Amos says it was the LORD who took him from following the flock and told him, “Go, prophesy to My people Israel.” (Amos 7:15) Amos doesn't name any king as the one who sent him. He names the LORD, and that settles it.

Not quite, friend. Amos is answering Amaziah, and he says, “You say: ‘Do not prophesy against Israel; do not preach against the house of Isaac.’” (Amos 7:16) The LORD's word that follows says “your wife” and “you yourself” (Amos 7:17), so it's pointed at the priest. Jeroboam is the one Amaziah wrote to (Amos 7:10), but he isn't the one being addressed here.

False is right. Amos has just been told to leave, and he says, “Now, therefore, hear the word of the LORD.” (Amos 7:16) Then he quotes what Amaziah said, and the LORD's word comes with “your wife” and “you yourself” (Amos 7:17). That's all aimed at the priest, not the king. Amaziah took his report to the king, but the LORD's word came to Amaziah.

Divided is right. The LORD's word to Amaziah says, “Your land will be divided by a measuring line…” (Amos 7:17) It comes right after Amos repeats what Amaziah said about not prophesying (Amos 7:16). This part of the passage is heavy, so I'll read it plainly and keep my voice down.

Sold isn't the word here. The LORD says, “Your land will be divided by a measuring line…” (Amos 7:17) Nobody is making an offer on it. The land is split up by a measuring line, and I'll leave that part quiet because it's a heavy one.

Guarded doesn't appear in this line. The word says, “Your land will be divided by a measuring line…” (Amos 7:17) There's no mention of guards, only of the land being divided. It's a heavy part of the story, so I'll say it plainly and keep going.

True. The LORD's word to Amaziah includes, “you yourself will die on pagan soil.” (Amos 7:17) It sits in the same word as the line about his land, and it ends with Israel going into exile. I think this one hurts to read, so I won't dress it up. Let's take it plainly.

The word says he will. The LORD tells Amaziah, “you yourself will die on pagan soil.” (Amos 7:17) It's right there in the same word as the line about his land. I think this one is hard to read, so I'll say it plainly and leave it there.
